name: Alhambra
label: Alhambra
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mirador de San Nicolás' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mirador de San Nicolás' (node/1213321729): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/92528618: large area 'Alhambra' (798 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The famous Nasrid palace and fortress complex above the city.

text.description:
The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex on a hill above Granada, and one of the best-known monuments of Islamic architecture. Building began in 1238 under Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, the first Nasrid ruler. The name comes from the Arabic for 'the red one', after the reddish walls of rammed earth. Over the centuries it grew into a small royal city with palaces, baths, towers and gates. The Alcazaba fortress sits at its western tip, and the Generalife, a former summer estate with gardens, lies just outside the walls to the east. A Renaissance palace was added in 1526 under Charles V, and today the whole site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The best way to photograph it on a phone is from across the Darro valley, where you can see the whole walled hill in one frame with the Sierra Nevada behind. The view is wide, so the red walls, towers and gardens all fit together. Stand off-centre and keep the low wall beside you to get the same view with fewer people in the shot. If you want a different angle, Mirador de San Cristóbal gives a wider view with much of the city in front. Puente de las Chirimías shows the Alhambra rising above the Darro valley, seen from below.
text.geographic_location: The Alhambra stands on Sabika hill on the edge of Granada, above the Darro valley. The viewpoint is across the valley, looking back at it.
text.directions_text: Head for Mirador de San Nicolás, across the Darro valley from the Alhambra. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Once you are on the square, the Alhambra is to the south-east, across the valley. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole Alhambra and Generalife with the Sierra Nevada behind. Then try 2x-3x (or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and palace walls. The ultra-wide (0.5x) tends to push the Alhambra into the distance and add a lot of foreground, so use it only if you want the crowd and the city in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mirador de San Nicolás (Left side of the esplanade as you face the Alhambra, near the low wall, not the centre). The classic frontal view of the Alhambra and Generalife across the Darro valley, with the Sierra Nevada behind. On the left side of the esplanade as you face the Alhambra, near the low wall rather than in the centre. From here you look south-east across the Darro valley to the classic frontal view of the Alhambra and Generalife, with the Sierra Nevada behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the line of the hill on the lower third, leaving room for the mountains above. Keep the low wall out of the frame, or let it appear as a simple strip at the bottom. For a different view, try Mirador de San Cristóbal for a wider shot with the city in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. For a wide sweep including the mountains, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or golden hour. The square fills up near sunset, so arrive well before then or stand off-centre.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is a public square, but check opening hours and access on the day; for the Alhambra itself, which may be ticketed or have timed entry, check the official site before you go.

name: El Bañuelo
label: El Bañuelo
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/182781541: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'El Bañuelo' (41 m across).
notes: 11th-century Arab baths on the Carrera del Darro.

text.description:
El Bañuelo is a preserved Islamic bathhouse (hammam) in Granada's Albaicín quarter, on the banks of the Darro River. It is traditionally dated to the 11th century, though some researchers think it is 12th century or later. It stayed in use as a bathhouse until the 16th century, and later served as a public laundry and then a dwelling. It was declared a Cultural Heritage Property of Spain in 1918, and it is now open to visitors. It is also the only restored hammam in Granada, outside the Alhambra, that the public can visit.

It photographs well because the rooms are laid out in a row, with columns and horseshoe arches that make natural frames. The largest room, the warm room, has a central vault resting on marble columns. Many of the column tops were reused from Roman and Caliphal buildings. The ceilings are pierced with small star-shaped and octagonal skylights, which let in thin beams of light and let steam escape. The first room, with its square water basin, is open to the sky today, though it once had a wooden dome.

Expect low light indoors, so keep your phone steady against a wall or column and take a couple of frames of each view. Look for repeating arches leading your eye down the rooms, and for the skylights as bright points in the vault. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any photography rules.
text.geographic_location: El Bañuelo is in the Albaicín quarter of Granada, on the banks of the Darro River.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is given for this spot, so head for the Albaicín quarter, on the banks of the Darro River. The bathhouse stands on the banks of the Darro River, so once you are in the Albaicín, look for the building beside the river. The phone icon on the map is at El Bañuelo, so follow the map on foot for the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the rooms and arches. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the smaller chambers where you cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for column tops and skylights.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Inside, take your main photos from the doorways between rooms, looking along the line of columns and horseshoe arches. In the open first room, stand back from the water basin so you can include it in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the arches symmetrically, so the columns sit either side of the frame. Include the water basin or the floor in the foreground for depth. For a detail shot, zoom in on a column top or a star-shaped skylight in the vault.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest skylight, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the vault keeps its detail and the light beams stay clear. If the room is very dark, try night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a wall to keep still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the skylights are bright, usually around the middle of the day, so that beams of light cross the dim rooms. Go early or late in the day for fewer people in your shots.

text.access_note: El Bañuelo is a historic site open to visitors, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements, tickets and photography rules.

name: Granada Cathedral
label: Granada Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de las Pasiegas' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de las Pasiegas' (relation/11490651): middle (66 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/124069145: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Catedral de Granada' (173 m across).
notes: Spanish Renaissance cathedral in the city centre.

text.description:
Granada Cathedral is the big Renaissance and Baroque church at the heart of the old city. It was begun in 1518 on the site of the city's main mosque, and it took 181 years to build. Diego de Siloé took over the design in 1529, and in 1667 Alonso Cano reworked the main façade with Baroque touches. The result is a tall front shaped like a triumphal arch, with three great arched openings. Two towers were planned at 81 metres each, but the project was left incomplete.

It photographs well because Plaza de las Pasiegas, directly in front, is an open pedestrian square, so you can see the whole façade without traffic in the way. Look for the pale stone arches and the carved details on the pillars. People walking across the square add a sense of scale.

If the square is busy, step to one side and wait a moment for a gap. During Holy Week, official stands are put up in the square and can block the view. For a different angle, Plaza de la Romanilla shows the cathedral behind palm trees.
text.geographic_location: In the old centre of Granada, on the site of the former main mosque in the heart of the old Muslim medina. The best front view is from Plaza de las Pasiegas, right beside the cathedral.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Granada and the cathedral, then walk into Plaza de las Pasiegas, the pedestrian square in front of the main west façade. There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head to the centre of Granada and walk to the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full façade in from the square. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a less stretched, more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details such as the arches and medallions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de las Pasiegas (directly in front of the main west façade). The full Baroque main façade of the cathedral, framed by the open pedestrian square. Directly in front of the main west façade. From here the full Baroque façade, designed by Alonso Cano, is framed by the open pedestrian square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone upright and level, so the vertical lines of the façade stay straight and don't lean inwards. Leave a little space around the top and sides so the building has room. For a simple alternative, Plaza de la Romanilla gives you the façade behind palm trees and the Aguador Monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Try the ultra-wide first, then compare it with the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the square is quieter, such as early in the day, for a clearer front view. Late afternoon may suit the west-facing front, but check the light when you arrive.

text.access_note: Plaza de las Pasiegas is an open pedestrian square, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: Sacromonte
label: Sacromonte
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mirador de San Miguel Alto' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mirador de San Miguel Alto' (node/2246108726): point.
notes: Hillside quarter known for its cave houses and flamenco.

text.description:
Sacromonte is the hillside neighbourhood in the east of Granada, facing the Alhambra across the valley of the Darro. It is known for its cave houses, dug into the slope and finished with whitewashed fronts. The caves are thought to date from the 16th century, and no two are the same, because each follows the shape of the hill. The area has long been associated with Granada's Romani community, who settled in the city after 1492. It also takes its name from the 'Lead Books' story of the late 1590s, which led to the building of the Abbey of Sacromonte in the 17th century.

It photographs well because the white houses, the olive-green slopes and the Alhambra all fit into one wide view. The most rewarding spot is a high terrace, the Mirador de San Miguel Alto, beside a hermitage. From there you look over the Sacromonte hillside to the Alhambra and the city below. It is a quieter, higher alternative to the lookouts closer to the houses. If you want the cave houses as the main subject, the Mirador de la Vereda de Enmedio shows them with the Alhambra behind.

The climb up is steep, so allow time and wear sensible shoes. Keep your phone and belongings close when you walk the lanes lower down.
text.geographic_location: Sacromonte is in the eastern part of Granada, on the hillside and valley opposite the Alhambra. It is part of the wider Albayzín district and borders the Albayzín itself.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Sacromonte borders the Albayzín. The final climb to the terrace is steep and on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of hillside, city and Alhambra. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Alhambra or a group of whitewashed houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mirador de San Miguel Alto. A high panorama across the Sacromonte hillside, with the Alhambra and the city below, taken from beside the hermitage. From here the photo shows a high panorama over the Sacromonte hillside, with the Alhambra and the city below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top third line, so the hillside and the Alhambra fill most of the picture. Use the nearest terrace edge or a hillside plant as a foreground to give a sense of depth. The Alhambra is the main target from this side, so for close shots of the cave houses, try the Mirador de la Vereda de Enmedio instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Alhambra to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for the widest sweep, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the recommended time. It can be busier then, so arrive early to get a good spot at the terrace.

text.access_note: The terrace itself is listed as free to visit, but if you plan to go into the Abbey of Sacromonte or the Sacromonte Caves Museum, check the official site before you go.

name: Generalife
label: Generalife
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mirador de San Nicolás' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mirador de San Nicolás' (node/1213321729): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/196490785: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Generalife' (396 m across).
notes: Summer palace with terraced gardens next to the Alhambra.

text.description:
The Generalife was the summer palace and country estate of the Nasrid rulers of Granada. It stands directly east of the Alhambra and uphill from it, so from across the valley it sits beside the red Alhambra walls with the mountains behind. Its gardens are laid out on three long terraces, each about 35 metres wide and 250 metres long, which gives the hillside a layered, green look even from far away. The palace is thought to date from the end of the 13th century, probably built under Muhammad II, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the Alhambra since 1984.

The most useful view for a phone photo is the outside one. From Mirador de San Nicolás, the small square in front of the San Nicolás church in the Albaicín, the Generalife sits on the left of the frame. The Alhambra towers, the Sierra Nevada and the city rooftops fill the rest. It is a free viewpoint and guides treat it as the classic exterior view, but it gets very crowded, with vendors nearby. Arrive early if you want a clear spot, and shoot a few frames at different zoom levels while you wait for the light. If you want a closer, upward-looking view, Mirador de los Carvajales is an alternative, showing the Generalife and the Alhambra's red walls from below.
text.geographic_location: The Generalife is on the hillside directly east of and uphill from the Alhambra, in Granada. The best outside view is from Mirador de San Nicolás in the Albaicín district, looking across the valley.
text.directions_text: Head for the Albaicín, the old district facing the Alhambra across the valley, and ask for Mirador de San Nicolás, the small square in front of the San Nicolás church. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The viewpoint is about 801 m north-west of the Generalife, in the Albaicín, so the Generalife is to the south-east as you look from the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole view of the Alhambra hill, mountains and city. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Generalife and its terraces. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the Generalife look very small, so save it for the rooftops and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mirador de San Nicolás (small square in front of the San Nicolás church, Albaicín). The Generalife on the left of the frame, with the Alhambra towers, the Sierra Nevada behind, and the city below. Look south-east across the valley. From here the Generalife sits on the left of the frame, with the Alhambra towers, the Sierra Nevada behind and the city below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the Generalife on the left third, with the Alhambra towers in the middle and the mountains along the top. Include a strip of rooftops at the bottom for depth. For a tighter picture, zoom to 3x or 5x and fill the frame with the walls and terraces. If you want a different angle, Mirador de los Carvajales looks up at the Generalife and the red walls from below.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Generalife to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the red walls. Hold the phone against the wall or your body when zooming, to keep the picture sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the light falls on the red walls. The viewpoint gets very crowded, so arrive early to get a good spot.

text.access_note: The Mirador de San Nicolás is a free open public square, but the gardens and palace of the Generalife need an Alhambra/Generalife ticket, so check the official site before you go, including any rules on tripods and professional gear.

name: Royal Chapel of Granada
label: Royal Chapel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Oficios' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Oficios nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/20774141: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Chapel' (77 m across).
notes: Burial place of the Catholic Monarchs.

text.description: The Royal Chapel of Granada (Capilla Real) is a late Gothic building, in the Isabelline style, built between 1505 and 1517 beside Granada Cathedral. It was planned as the burial place of Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand, the Catholic Monarchs, and their tomb is still here. For a phone camera, the chapel's best side is its street front. The stonework is detailed, and the narrow street frames it neatly, so a simple straight-on shot already looks good. Try one wide shot to show the entrance in its setting, then a closer one of the carving. Photography is prohibited inside the chapel, so this exterior is the picture to take. If you want the chapel together with the cathedral next door, walk to the open Plaza de la Catedral for a wider view. Next to the chapel you can also see the Lonja, a building from 1518 that was once used for banking and commerce. The chapel is still used for Catholic worship and is sometimes closed to visitors, so check the official site before you go. Morning light suits the façade best, and early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stone.
text.geographic_location: In the old centre of Granada, attached to the cathedral.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head for Granada Cathedral in the city centre, where the Royal Chapel is built against it, and walk the rest. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too tight to fit the entrance in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Oficios (opposite the chapel's small Plateresque façade on Oficios Street). The chapel's carved Plateresque entrance and its surrounding decorative details, framed by the street. Opposite the chapel's small Plateresque façade. From here you see the carved entrance and the decoration around it, framed by the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the doorway up with a central line so the carving looks balanced. Keep the phone level and don't tilt it up too far, or the walls will lean inwards. Then zoom in for a close shot of the carved stonework. For a wider alternative that includes the neighbouring cathedral, take a shot from Plaza de la Catedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sunlit carving looks washed out or the sky is bright. Take a few shots, because passers-by often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when sun falls on the façade. Early morning or late afternoon also gives soft light on the stonework.

text.access_note: The chapel is a place of worship and a visitor attraction, and photography is prohibited inside; the street outside is open to the public, but check the official site before you go for visiting times, tickets and dress code.

name: Parque de las Ciencias (Granada)
label: Parque de las Ciencias
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Edificio Macroscopio' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Edificio Macroscopio' (way/51729476): middle (286 m across); moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24479691: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parque de las Ciencias' (509 m across).

text.description:
Parque de las Ciencias is Granada's big science museum, and it works well as a photo stop because it is as much about architecture and gardens as exhibits. The park covers 70,000 square metres, and about 27,000 of those are garden, with outdoor exhibits that make the most of the Andalusian weather. A strong picture is of the Macroscopio, the newer main building. It was designed by the architect Carlos Ferrater as an expansion of the original museum. Seen from its outdoor approach, the building appears to be framed against the gardens and ornamental fountains, so you can get strong shapes, water and greenery in one frame.

The older Foucault Pendulum building opened in May 1995 and holds the planetarium, which has a 10 m dome. It is a good second subject if you want a different look at the park's architecture.

For a phone photo, stand back far enough to include both the building and some foreground water or planting. Keep the phone level, using gridlines to keep the edges of the building straight, and take a few frames at slightly different distances. If you have time, there are two other spots to try: the Plaza Marie Curie, for the open-air side of the park, and the Einstein sculpture by Miguel Barranco at the entrance, for a close-up with the gateway behind it.
text.geographic_location: Parque de las Ciencias is in Granada, a large museum-and-garden site. The photo spot is on the open approach in front of the main building, the Macroscopio.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so check a map or the park's official site for the best way to get there and ask for Parque de las Ciencias. Once inside the grounds, make for the Macroscopio, the park's main building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole Macroscopio and its fountains into one frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the building's edges and the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (outdoor approach in front of the main building). The park's main building, the Macroscopio, framed against its outdoor gardens and ornamental fountains. From here the park's main building appears to be framed against its gardens and ornamental fountains, and the wider grounds lie to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's main edges up with them so the walls stay straight. Include a strip of fountain or planting in the foreground to give depth, and keep the phone level rather than tilting it up. For a second picture, try the Plaza Marie Curie for the open-air side of the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly if the sky is washing out. If the fountains are running, a Live Photo can catch the movement of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the building. Check the park's opening times on the official site before you go.

text.access_note: The museum and its outdoor areas may be ticketed separately, so check the official site before you go to see whether the gardens and the approach are free to enter.

name: Alcaicería of Granada
label: Alcaicería
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Alcaicería' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Alcaicería nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1381852660: the OpenStreetMap point 'Alcaicería'.
notes: Old Moorish silk market, now a bazaar of narrow lanes.

text.description:
The Alcaicería is a small network of narrow market lanes in the historic centre of Granada, now lined with shops. It stands on the site of the old Nasrid silk bazaar, which was locked and guarded at night. That bazaar burned down in 1843, and the market was rebuilt on a much smaller scale in a Neo-Moorish style that imitates Nasrid architecture. A plan from 1787 shows up to 152 shops, so today's lanes are only a remnant of the original.

For photographs, the best picture is the Moorish-style entrance arch on Calle Alcaicería. From the north side, facing south, the arch frames the Cathedral tower, and the narrow lane leads your eye in. The arch, the lane and the tower give you a layered shot that works well on a phone screen. The other entrance has a second archway with patterned details and colourful shop fronts behind it, which makes a good alternative.

Go early if you can. Guides suggest the arch looks best in the morning before about 10 am, when the shops are shut and the lanes are quiet. After about 11 am, crowds and street stalls can spoil the composition. Photography is generally fine in the alleys, but be discreet with shop owners and other visitors, and ask before pointing your phone at people working in their shops.
text.geographic_location: In the historic heart of Granada, just south-west of the Cathedral, in the area bounded by Calle Libreros, Calle Oficios, Calle Tinte, Calle Zacatín and Plaza Bibarrambla.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or rail stop at this spot, so head on foot for the Cathedral and Plaza Bibarrambla area in the centre of Granada. The Alcaicería lies just south-west of the Cathedral. Once you are at the north entrance arch on Calle Alcaicería, the Alcaicería is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the arch, the lane and the Cathedral tower in one frame. Try 2x or more to bring the tower closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful if you want more of the arch's patterned detail and the shop fronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Alcaicería (north entrance arch, facing south toward the Cathedral). The Moorish-style entrance arch framing the Cathedral tower in the background, with the narrow market lane leading in. On Calle Alcaicería, at the north entrance arch, facing south toward the Cathedral. The arch should frame the Cathedral tower, with the narrow market lane leading in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and centre the arch so the tower sits in the opening. Keep your phone level so the lane's sides stay straight. If you have time, walk to the market's other entrance for the second Moorish-style archway, with its patterned details and colourful shop fronts. Check that entrance on the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch or the tower to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright sky behind the tower keeps some detail. If the lane is crowded, take a few frames in a row or a short Live Photo and choose the cleanest one afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before 10 am, before the shops open and the foot traffic arrives. After about 11 am the lane gets busy and stalls can get in the way.

text.access_note: The lanes are an open market street with shops, so be discreet and considerate when photographing; check the official site (alcaiceria.com) before you go.

photo.artist: Jesus Abizanda from Barbastro, Huesca, Spain

name: Palace of Charles V
label: Palace of Charles V
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palacio de Carlos V' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Palacio de Carlos V' (relation/2640220): middle (103 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2640220: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palace of Charles V' (103 m across).
notes: Renaissance palace with a circular courtyard inside the Alhambra.

text.description:
The Palace of Charles V is a Renaissance building standing inside the Alhambra, on the Sabika hill. Its plain, heavy stone looks very different from the Moorish palaces around it, which is why it makes such a striking photo. Work began in 1527 to designs by Pedro Machuca, who had trained in Italy. It stopped for good in 1637, and the building had no roof until 1967. From the outside it looks like a big square block, about 63 metres along each side and 17 metres high, with rough-cut stone on the lower storey and a more elegant upper floor above. Inside is a surprising round courtyard. Today the palace houses the Alhambra Museum on the ground floor and the Fine Arts Museum of Granada upstairs.

For your photo, stand and face the west façade, the palace's main front. From there you can capture the stone walls, the columns, the carved medallions and the grand doorway, with the Alhambra's gardens around it. Step back as far as the space allows so the whole front fits, and keep your phone upright so the walls stay straight. If you go inside, the round courtyard with its two tiers of columns is the best alternative. For a wider view of the whole Alhambra, with the palace as a small part of the scene, try Mirador de San Nicolás.
text.geographic_location: The palace stands in the middle of the Alhambra complex, on the Sabika hill above central Granada. It sits beside the older Nasrid palaces and the gardens around them.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near this spot, so check the Alhambra's official site for how to reach the complex. Once inside, follow the signs to the Palace of Charles V. The west façade is the side to shoot from. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) and stand as far back as the space allows. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the façade will not fit. Use telephoto (2x or more) for close shots of the medallions and the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (west façade (the palace's main façade, with the monumental doorway), shot from the forecourt in front of it). The rusticated stone exterior with its columns, carved medallions and entrance, framed against the Alhambra's surrounding gardens. Step back onto the open space in front of the west façade if the whole front does not fit. From here you see the rusticated stone exterior with its columns, carved medallions and entrance, framed against the Alhambra's surrounding gardens.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the monumental doorway and turn on gridlines, so the vertical lines of the walls stay straight. Keep the phone level rather than tilting it up, or the building will seem to lean back. Include some of the gardens at the edge of the frame for context. For a different view, the round courtyard inside gives a symmetrical shot of the two tiers of columns, and Mirador de San Nicolás gives a distant view of the whole Alhambra.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the carved details do not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour before sunset, when the warm light brings out the colour of the stone.

text.access_note: The palace is inside the Alhambra complex and entry rules differ for the façade, the courtyard and the museums, so check the official site before you go.

Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep detail in the stone when the sky is bright.

name: Court of the Lions
label: Court of the Lions
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4270926: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Iconic courtyard with the lion fountain.

text.description:
The Court of the Lions is the courtyard at the centre of the Palace of the Lions, in the heart of the Alhambra in Granada. It was commissioned by the Nasrid sultan Muhammad V and built during his second reign, between 1362 and 1391. The courtyard is rectangular, with a marble fountain in the middle held up by twelve sculpted lions. Four main halls open off it, and water channels link the central fountain to smaller fountains inside them. The halls are known for some of the most elaborate muqarnas (stalactite-like) vaults in the Islamic world. The name 'Lions' is a modern one, taken from the sculptures. Together with the Alhambra, the palace is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

It photographs well because it is a compact, symmetrical space with a clear centrepiece. The fountain gives you an obvious subject, and the surrounding arcades and carved detail give you layers to work with. Start with a wide view that shows the whole court and the fountain, then move closer for the lions and the carved decoration. The Hall of the Two Sisters stands on the north side of the court, which makes a useful reference point when you line up a shot. Expect other visitors in the frame, so be patient and shoot in the gaps between groups. Access to the palace may be ticketed or timed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of the Alhambra, the palace-and-fortress complex in Granada. The court sits next to the Comares Palace to the west, and the Lindaraja courtyard lies to the north.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or similar stop at this spot, so check local options for reaching the Alhambra in Granada. Once inside the Alhambra, make your way to the Palace of the Lions, in the heart of the complex. The phone icon on the map is in the courtyard itself, so there is no extra walk once you are inside. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole court and the fountain into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the fountain and arcades. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the lions and the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand beside the fountain and face north towards the Hall of the Two Sisters, or turn around to shoot along the other sides of the court.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use them to keep the arcades and the fountain straight, as the court is very symmetrical. Place the fountain in the centre for a formal, balanced shot, or stand off to one side and use the arcade as a foreground frame. Take one wide shot, then a closer shot of the lions with the telephoto. For ceilings and vaults, hold the phone level and shoot upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sunlit stone does not wash out. Go back inside the halls and tap on the shaded areas to lift the detail there. Skip portrait mode for the architecture, and try a short Live Photo of the fountain if you like.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit at the start or end of your slot if you can, when there tend to be fewer people. Soft, even daylight is easiest for the carved stone, while strong midday sun can leave deep shadows in the arcades.

text.access_note: The Court of the Lions is part of the Alhambra, which may be ticketed or have timed entry, so check the official site before you go.

name: Alcazaba of the Alhambra
label: Alcazaba
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mirador de San Nicolás' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mirador de San Nicolás' (node/1213321729): point.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Alcazaba of the Alhambra'.
notes: The oldest part of the Alhambra, with sweeping views over the city.

text.description:
The Alcazaba is the fortress at the western tip of the Alhambra hill in Granada, and the oldest surviving part of the whole Alhambra. Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid dynasty, built it after 1238 on the site of an earlier 11th-century fortress. Its plan is roughly a triangle, with the Torre de la Vela at the western corner, the Torre del Homenaje (26 m tall) at the north-east and the Torre Hueca at the south-east. The walls are mostly rammed earth. Warm sunset light brings out the red tones of the walls.

The best way to photograph it is from across the valley, at the Mirador de San Nicolás, a terrace in the Albaicín that faces the Alhambra hill. From here you see the whole hill head-on, with the Alcazaba and palace towers along the ridge and the Sierra Nevada behind. Guides call it the classic postcard view, so it gets very busy, especially around sunset. Arrive early if you want room at the railing.

The Alcazaba is a fortress and a strong, simple shape, so it works well in a wide frame with the mountains behind. If you want a different angle, the Mirador de los Carvajales gives a view of the Alhambra framed by overhanging leaves. Whichever you choose, keep your phone steady against the railing or a wall, and take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
text.geographic_location: The Alcazaba sits at the western tip of the Alhambra hill in Granada. The viewpoint is on a terrace in the Albaicín district, facing the Alhambra hill.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Granada and head for the Albaicín, the old district on the hill facing the Alhambra, then look for the Mirador de San Nicolás. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole Alhambra hill with the Sierra Nevada behind. Then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Alcazaba's towers and walls from the rest of the complex.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mirador de San Nicolás (north-facing terrace in the Albaicín, facing the Alhambra hill). The Alhambra hill seen frontally, with the Alcazaba and palace towers in view and the Sierra Nevada behind. The north-facing terrace in the Albaicín, and face south-east. From there the Alhambra hill is seen frontally, with the Alcazaba and palace towers in view and the Sierra Nevada behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the hill on the lower third, leaving the sky and mountains above. Zoom in a little to make the Alcazaba the main subject rather than a small part of a wide view. If the railing is crowded, the Mirador de los Carvajales is an alternative, where overhanging leaves frame the view of the Alhambra.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the walls do not wash out. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for when you want the whole hill and sky, but expect the fortress to look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset for warm light on the red walls, or early morning for fewer people.

text.access_note: The Mirador de San Nicolás is an open public terrace, but entering the Alcazaba is part of the Alhambra visit, so check the official site before you go.

name: Puerta Real (Granada)
label: Puerta Real
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida de los Reyes Católicos' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Calle Reyes Católicos' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24379213: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puerta Real' (86 m across).
notes: Central square at the heart of modern Granada.

text.description:
Puerta Real is the busy open square at the heart of Granada's city centre, in the historic area that includes Recogidas Street, Reyes Católicos Street and Carrera de la Virgen. The gate that gave it its name no longer stands, so what you photograph today is the square and the streets around it. It is a good place for a city-life shot: wide open space in the foreground, then long street frontages and a lively edge of cafés and shops.

The name goes back to King Philip IV's visit on 8 April 1624. In the 16th century the square became the centre of Granada's social life, and in 1515 it was decorated with the Catholic Monarchs' coat of arms. The Darro River once ran through here until it was enclosed in the 19th century for reasons of hygiene. After that, Puerta Real grew more popular than Elvira Street and Plaza Nueva as a place to meet.

For the classic view, stand on Avenida de los Reyes Católicos and look back across the square towards the start of the avenue. Keeping the open space in the foreground gives the picture depth and a wider street perspective than a view from inside the square. The square has a fountain (Fuente de las Batallas) and a kiosk, and either can block an angle, so take a few steps left or right until the view clears. A second option is from the square itself, with the Café Suizo building and the surrounding frontages as your backdrop.
text.geographic_location: Puerta Real is in the city centre of Granada, in the historic area that includes Reyes Católicos Street, Recogidas Street and Carrera de la Virgen.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Granada and ask for Puerta Real or Calle de los Reyes Católicos. Stand and face south-west across the square to take the view. Do not walk into the square and turn round, as that would point you away from it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives a natural view of the square and the avenue. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit in more of the street frontages and the open foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the Café Suizo building or the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida de los Reyes Católicos. A view across Puerta Real toward the start of the Reyes Católicos avenue, with the square's open space in the foreground. Which lies to the south-west. From here you see across Puerta Real towards the start of the avenue, with the square's open space in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the avenue's line of buildings along one of the vertical lines so the street runs neatly into the picture. Keep a band of open square at the bottom of the frame for depth. If the kiosk or fountain gets in the way, shift a few steps sideways. For a different view, step into the square and frame the Café Suizo building and the surrounding frontages as your backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop bright sky from darkening the street. Take a few frames in a row, as people and traffic keep moving through the scene. Try a short Live Photo to capture the movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: Puerta Real is a city square and street area, so it should be open to walk around freely; check the official site before you go if you need anything more specific.
claims_not_in_sources: The square and avenue are open public space that can be visited at any time.
Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and fewer people.
The area is busy with pedestrians and traffic during the day.
Night mode works best if the phone is held steady against a wall or railing.

name: Madrasa of Granada
label: Madrasa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Oficios' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Oficios nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/124074945: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Madrasah of Granada' (62 m across).
notes: Former Nasrid university with an ornate prayer hall.

text.description:
The Madrasa of Granada, also called the Madraza, is a university building on Calle Oficios, in the old centre close to the Cathedral. It began in 1349 as a college founded by the Nasrid ruler Yusuf I, and it is the only major madrasa known to have been built in al-Andalus. Most of that first building was pulled down between 1722 and 1729 and replaced by a Baroque town hall designed by José de Bada. What you see from the street is therefore mainly an 18th-century front. Inside, the 14th-century prayer room survives, a square room about 6.8 metres a side with fine stucco work. The building has belonged to the University of Granada since 1976.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the dark stone facade with its ironwork, lanterns and carved Baroque window surrounds, set inside a narrow street. The street is also the difficulty. It is tight, so a straight-on wide shot is hard, and the Cathedral and Royal Chapel bring people past all day. Aim for a diagonal view along the street, with the facade running into the picture, and use close-ups for the details. Keep your phone level so the walls do not lean too much. If the front is covered or closed for work when you visit, photograph the street scene and the details you can still see.
text.geographic_location: In the old centre of Granada, on Calle Oficios, a short walk from the Cathedral and the Alcaicería, the old silk bazaar quarter.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is given for this spot, so head for the Cathedral area in the old centre, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. Calle Oficios is the street beside the Cathedral and the Royal Chapel. Walk up it from the Gran Vía end and the Madraza is on the left-hand side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade into the narrow street, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the ironwork, lanterns and window decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Oficios (Walking up from the Gran Vía end, the Madraza is on the left-hand side of the street). The dark ashlar facade of the Madraza with its ironwork, lanterns and Baroque window decoration, framed by the narrow street. From here the photo shows the dark stone facade with its ironwork, lanterns and Baroque window decoration, framed by the narrow street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the street walls as guide lines leading to the facade. Keep the phone upright and level so the building does not lean. Take one wider shot for context, then step in for close-ups of the lanterns and windows. With the Cathedral and Royal Chapel on the same street, wait for gaps in the passing crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the bright sky is washing out the dark stone. In dim light, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you can, when fewer people are in the street. Come back around dusk to try the lanterns with night mode.

text.access_note: You can see the facade from the public street, but inside visits need advance registration at the Madraza information point, and the front may be under renovation, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The street is narrow, so direct light on the facade is limited and a wide shot is difficult.
Early in the day the street is usually quieter.
The lanterns may be lit around dusk.
Ultra-wide shots taken close to a building can make vertical lines lean inwards.

name: Corral del Carbón
label: Corral del Carbón
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Reyes Católicos' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Reyes Católicos nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2788286: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Corral del Carbón' (60 m across).

text.description: The Corral del Carbón is a 14th-century building that began as a Nasrid inn and warehouse for grain and for merchants from outside the city. It is the only building of its kind from that period still standing in the Iberian Peninsula. Later it served as a theatre courtyard and then as housing, and its present name, 'Courtyard of Coal', comes from the coal that was weighed and stored on the ground floor. The front is what makes it photograph well. A tall projecting gateway holds the doors under a large vaulted recess. Above the doorway sit carved arch patterns, a band of Arabic lettering, a double-arched window and panels of fine plaster carving, all topped by a wooden eaves. Behind it, the courtyard is almost square, about 17 by 16 metres, with a stone basin in the middle and galleries around it. That gives a more relaxed picture than standing square-on, and the street itself adds context. If you want the classic straight-on view of the gateway, take it from the street in front of the doorway. If you go in, you can also shoot the arch from inside, with the gallery edge in the frame for scale. Keep your phone steady and take a few frames, as people pass constantly.
text.geographic_location: In the old centre of Granada, just south of the Albaicín and close to the Cathedral. The official page lists the building's address as Calle Mariana Pineda 12, while another guide places it near Reyes Católicos 28.
text.directions_text: Head to the Cathedral area in the centre of Granada. The Corral del Carbón is a short walk from the Cathedral. Note that the official page lists its address as Calle Mariana Pineda 12, while another guide places it near Reyes Católicos 28. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the oblique view of the frontage. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the whole gateway. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the inscription band and the carved panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Reyes Católicos (the projecting stretch of the street near number 28, looking at the building's frontage). A more oblique street-level view of the building's frontage set into the main shopping street, rather than the portal head-on. The building lies to the south-east of you. From here you see the frontage side-on, set into the main shopping street, rather than the doorway head-on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the edge of the gateway up with a vertical grid line so the walls do not lean. Let the street run into the frame to show the building in its setting. For the head-on version, an alternative is to photograph the arched doorway straight from the street in front of it, or from inside, with the gallery edge in the frame and the bright street beyond the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stucco and tilework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky and street do not wash out the details. Use the 2x lens, not digital zoom beyond it, for close-ups of the lettering.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the street is likely to be quieter and the light softer.

text.access_note: The building is a historic site and the visit covers only the ground floor, so check the official site before you go for access and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Calle Reyes Católicos is a busy shopping street, so there are likely to be passers-by in the frame.
The street may be too narrow to fit the whole gateway with the default lens (1x), so the ultra-wide lens may help.

name: Gate of Elvira
label: Puerta de Elvira
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza del Triunfo' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza del Triunfo' (way/157833176): middle (79 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/877866023: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puerta de Elvira' (7 m across).

text.description:
The Gate of Elvira (Puerta de Elvira) is an arch at the start of Calle Elvira, on the edge of the Albaicín neighbourhood. It began as part of the 11th-century Zirid walls. In the 14th century it was rebuilt as a heavily fortified gate, so it could join the new Nasrid extension of the walls. Only part of it survives, but the arch is still a strong, simple subject. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1896. Outside the gate there used to be a large Muslim burial ground, the Ibn Malik Cemetery, and the Royal Hospital now stands over part of it.

For a phone photo, the classic view is straight on from Plaza del Triunfo. The square gives you the whole front of the arch, framed by the buildings around it. Some of those buildings partly block the view, so check the framing and step back towards the edges of the square for a cleaner picture. If you want something calmer, the Jardines del Triunfo give a more open, quieter backdrop. Calle Elvira shows the gate closing the far end of the narrow, shop-lined street. Traffic and people pass through all of these places, so take a moment to frame the shot and wait for a gap. Late afternoon light is kind to the stonework.
text.geographic_location: The gate is in central Granada, at the beginning of Calle Elvira on the edge of the Albaicín neighbourhood. It stands on Plaza del Triunfo, next to the Jardines del Triunfo.
text.directions_text: No nearby Underground stations or tram stops are listed, so head for the start of Calle Elvira, on the edge of the Albaicín. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural frontal view of the arch. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if buildings or people force you to stand close. Use 2x if you step back to the edge of the square and want to fill the frame with the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza del Triunfo (in front of the gate, on the square's side facing the arch). The full front elevation of the Puerta de Elvira arch, framed by the square and the surrounding buildings. On the side of the square facing the arch, with the gate to the south. From here you see the full front of the Puerta de Elvira, framed by the square and the buildings around it. The Jardines del Triunfo give a more open, quieter alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arch up with the central vertical line so it looks straight. Keep your phone level to avoid leaning walls. If a nearby building cuts into the view, move sideways or back to the edges of the square. For a second photo, try Calle Elvira, with the gate closing the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stonework keeps its colour. Wait for gaps in the traffic and crowds rather than trying to edit them out afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the soft golden light flatters the stonework.

text.access_note: The gate is on an open public square and street, but Holy Week processions pass under the arch and may restrict access on those days, so check locally before you go.

name: Monasterio de San Jerónimo, Granada
label: San Jerónimo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Monasterio de San Jerónimo' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Monasterio de San Jerónimo' (relation/10371110): middle (137 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/218338748: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Real Monasterio de San Jerónimo' (221 m across).
notes: Renaissance monastery with a richly painted church.

text.description: The Royal Monastery of San Jerónimo is a Renaissance monastery and church in Granada, founded by the Catholic Monarchs. The buildings in the city began in 1504, and Diego de Siloé was the main architect and sculptor. The church is said to be the first in the world consecrated to the Immaculate Conception of Mary, and the Gran Capitán, Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, is buried in it. For photographs, the open forecourt (the compás) is the best place to start. It gives you a clear, uncluttered view of the carved Renaissance portal and façade, with the bell tower rising above. The tower is a good detail to include. French troops pulled the original down in the Napoleonic era, and it was only rebuilt in the 1980s, finished in 1989. Standing back in the forecourt lets you fit the whole portal in one frame. A second good picture is the large monumental gate on Calle Rector López Argüeta, where the ornate carving stands out against plain stone walls. That gate is original to the monastery, though it was lost for a time and returned to its place in the 1960s. Keep your phone level and step back until the tower sits comfortably in the top of the frame. Then move in for a few close shots of the carving. The cloisters, church and altarpiece are inside and ticketed, and photography rules there may differ, so check before you go in.
text.geographic_location: The monastery is in the city of Granada, on the side of Calle Rector López Argüeta.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station is listed for this spot, so head to Calle Rector López Argüeta, beside the monastery, and check the map as you arrive. The street name for the forecourt is not always given consistently (you may also see Compás de San Jerónimo). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the portal and façade as a whole. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the tower and the full width of the forecourt, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the compás forecourt, facing the church portal and façade). The Renaissance church portal and façade framed by the open forecourt, with the bell tower visible above. From here the Renaissance portal is framed by the open space, with the bell tower visible above it. The middle of the monastery lies to the north-east. If you want a different view, the monumental gate on Calle Rector López Argüeta is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the portal with the central vertical lines so the façade does not lean. Keep the phone upright, not tilted upwards, as far as you can, to stop the walls from slanting. Leave a little space above the tower. For a second picture, move to the gate on Calle Rector López Argüeta and shoot the carved decoration against the plain stone walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone of the portal to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright so the carving keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light on stone and fewer people in the forecourt.

text.access_note: The forecourt and street are outside, but the cloister, church and altarpiece are ticketed and only the first floor is open to visitors, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: The Church of San Salvador stands in the Albaicín, the old hillside quarter of Granada. It was built in the 16th century on the site of the neighbourhood's former main mosque, and part of that mosque survives: its courtyard, lined with horseshoe arches, is now part of the church. For a phone photo, the best thing here is the entrance portal. It was finished in 1543 in the ornate Granadan Plateresque style, under the direction of Diego Siloe, and was restored in 1996 as part of a restoration of the front. Beside it rises the bell tower, completed around 1592. Together they make a solid, tidy frontal shot, with warm stone and carved detail to fill the frame. The church also has a hard history: a fire in 1936 destroyed most of the building, and it was rebuilt afterwards. That makes the old portal and the courtyard arches all the more interesting to look at. The square in front is small and the street is steep and narrow, so you may not be able to step back as far as you would like. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) when you need to fit the portal and tower in together, and switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If you want a wider view over the rooftops, the Mirador de la Cruz de la Rauda is a good alternative, with the church near the middle of the picture and the Alhambra beyond.
text.geographic_location: In the Albaicín, the historic hillside district of Granada, at Plaza del Salvador just off Cuesta del Chapiz.
text.directions_text: No tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so head for Plaza del Salvador, which is reached off Cuesta del Chapiz. The final approach is on foot along steep, narrow streets, so expect a climb near the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on shot of the portal. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is too tight to fit the portal and bell tower together. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the carved detail of the doorway and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza del Salvador (directly in front of the church's main façade, reached off Cuesta del Chapiz). The church's Plateresque Renaissance entrance portal and bell tower, framed by the square in front of the building. From here you see the Plateresque Renaissance entrance portal and the bell tower, framed by the square in front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the portal up with the central vertical line so the stonework looks straight. Keep your phone level rather than tilting it upwards, as tilting makes the walls lean. If the square feels too tight, step to one side and use 0.5x, or take the tower and the portal as two separate photos. For a different view, the Mirador de la Cruz de la Rauda gives a raised look over the Albaicín rooftops with the Alhambra beyond. It involves a climb, as it is reached by steps down from San Miguel Alto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Phone cameras often overexpose pale stone against a bright sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: On a sunny day, early morning or later afternoon is kinder to the stone than the harsh light of midday. Try a quick test shot first.

text.access_note: The square is open to walk into, but the church is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and dress expectations.
